plan:
1. Two kinds of response really do protect you, more often than not. One is on duty all the time. It can sound like a skeptic, or like a critic watching you for weakness; one kind a reader would recognize is enough. It may have spent years keeping old hurts from happening again, like being humiliated or being left. It has probably watched you start other healing things full of excitement and then drop them. It may be tired, but it's experienced and good at what it does.
2. The other kind shows up when pain gets close: a sudden pull to do anything but feel it, anywhere from numbing out to keeping busy. One or two pulls a reader would recognize from having been there are enough, and not the phone or the laundry, which the article already used. It may be stepping in because nothing else seems able to hold what's coming up.
3. Both kinds usually grew up around trying to prevent something, like being humiliated or losing control, even when what they do now hurts you. Treating the response as an enemy, or as a failing of yours, usually gives it one more reason to stay in charge.
established:
- Start With Whatever Showed Up (just before this) says a reaction that shows up when you go looking for your little one counts as part of the work; it could be your little one, a part of you that's trying to protect you, the parent you inherited, or something from today. It tells the reader to ask what the reaction is trying to stop or wants, not to force past it, and to wait and listen.
- The article's words for the inside of a person: "part of you", "your little one", "the grown-up"/"the adult", "the inherited critic voice", and the grown-up's three functions, the Nurturer, the Protector and the Guide. "The Protector" is the grown-up's own protecting function, so a protective response is "a part of you that's trying to protect you" or "a protective part", never "the Protector".
- Examples the article already used for a reaction that gets in the way: the phone or the laundry suddenly feeling urgent, a voice saying this is silly, getting mad instead, staring at the rug.
limits:
- No list of three or more in one sentence (Joel, 2026-10-03: "lists of 3 in general are an ai pattern"). If a list doesn't need all its items, keep the one or two that matter most; if every item matters, give each its own sentence.
- Plain words. No labels like "proactive" and "reactive" unless a plain word says what they mean.
- Invent nothing about Joel's life, and no made-up scene longer than a small example.
- Every sentence has to work for a reader who doesn't remember anything from sections back.
- If a point seems to need one more condition, make the paragraph simpler rather than longer.
after: The next section, "A Bottom-Up Sequence", starts: notice the protective part, and don't push through it.
